sections.html:
Residential rentals in Nebraska fall under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, found in Chapter 76 of the Nebraska Revised Statutes starting at section 76-1401. It follows a tenancy from start to finish: the rental agreement, deposits, repairs, entry, termination, and the court case to recover possession.

For an owner thinking about a sale, the sections that come up most are these. Section 76-1416 covers security deposits and prepaid rent. Section 76-1417 requires disclosure of the manager and of the owner or owner's agent. Section 76-1419 makes the landlord keep the premises fit, and 76-1425 deals with landlord noncompliance. Section 76-1431 covers tenant noncompliance and failure to pay rent, 76-1434 bars landlord liens and distraint, and 76-1439 prohibits retaliation. Sections 76-1440 to 76-1447 run the action for possession from complaint to appeal.

Owners often ask whether listing a house ends a lease. Nothing in these sections says so, so check the lease itself and talk to an attorney before you assume a sale changes a tenant's rights.

sections.h2: Security deposits when a rental is sold
sections.html:
Whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends is bound by the deposit rules. Section 76-1416(5) says so directly. A seller should settle the deposit with the buyer at closing, in writing, so the new owner knows exactly what is being held.

The deposit rules are specific.

  • The landlord applies prepaid rent and security to unpaid rent and to damage caused by the tenant's breach, then returns any balance with a written itemization within fourteen days after the tenancy ends.
  • If the tenant gave no forwarding address, the landlord mails the balance and itemization to the last-known address by first-class mail.
  • Money that comes back undeliverable, or stays unclaimed for one year, is treated as abandoned property reported to the State Treasurer.
  • A landlord who misses the deadline can owe the tenant the money plus court costs and reasonable attorney's fees. If the failure is willful and not in good faith, the tenant can also recover liquidated damages equal to one month's rent or twice the deposit, whichever is less.

A cash buyer taking over a rental with tenants in place will usually ask for the lease, the deposit amount and the payment ledger. Having those ready speeds the closing.

sections.h2: Telling the tenant who owns and manages the home
sections.html:
Section 76-1417 requires the landlord, or whoever signs the rental agreement for the landlord, to give the tenant two names and addresses in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy. One is the person authorized to manage the premises. The other is an owner, or a person authorized to act for the owner, who accepts service of process and receives notices and demands.

When a rental changes hands, the tenant's rent and notices can suddenly go to the wrong place. The statute speaks to the start of a tenancy and does not describe a handover, but a seller and buyer should still give the tenant the new contact details in writing. That keeps rent, repair requests and notices from getting lost.

sections.h2: Ending a tenancy for nonpayment or breach
sections.html:
Nebraska uses a short notice for unpaid rent and a longer one for other breaches, both set out in section 76-1431. If rent is unpaid when due and the tenant does not pay within seven calendar days after written notice of nonpayment and of the landlord's intent to terminate, the landlord may end the rental agreement.

For a material breach, or a breach that affects health and safety, the landlord delivers a written notice naming the acts or omissions. It says the agreement ends on a date not less than thirty days after receipt unless the tenant fixes the problem within fourteen days. If substantially the same breach returns within six months, the landlord may end the agreement on at least fourteen days' written notice.

SituationWritten notice period
Rent unpaidSeven calendar days to pay
Material breach, first timeFourteen days to remedy; termination no sooner than thirty days after receipt
Same breach repeats within six monthsAt least fourteen days

These notices come before court. The Nebraska Judicial Branch adds that notice must be given to the adverse party three days before a forcible entry and detainer action is commenced (section 25-21,221). The act also gives tenants remedies for unlawful ouster and exclusion in section 76-1430, so shortcuts around the court process are risky.

sections.h2: When the landlord fails to keep the home livable
sections.html:
Section 76-1425 gives the tenant a mirror-image remedy. For a material noncompliance by the landlord, or a failure to meet the repair duty in section 76-1419 that materially affects health and safety, the tenant may give written notice listing the problem. If it is not fixed within fourteen days, the rental agreement ends on a date not less than thirty days after the landlord receives the notice. A repeat within six months allows termination on at least fourteen days' notice.

For a seller this matters because deferred repairs on a rental can leave a tenant with a legal claim against the owner at the same moment a buyer is inspecting. A written repair history helps both sides. The act has separate sections on failure to supply heat, water and essential services (76-1427), fire or casualty damage (76-1429), and tenant remedies for unlawful ouster or diminished service (76-1430).

sections.h2: Retaliation and seizing a tenant's belongings
sections.html:
A landlord may do neither, with limits. Section 76-1439 bars retaliation by raising rent, cutting services, or bringing or threatening an action for possession after a tenant complains to a government agency that enforces housing or building codes about a health or safety violation, or after the tenant joins or organizes a tenants' union. A tenant who is retaliated against has the remedies in section 76-1430 and a defense in an eviction case. Reasonable rent increases and changes in services remain allowed.

Section 76-1434 adds that a landlord's lien or security interest in a tenant's household goods cannot be enforced, and that distraint for rent is abolished. An owner preparing a rental for sale should never hold a tenant's property as leverage for unpaid rent.

The act also has special rules for tenants who are victims of domestic violence, including release from the rental agreement and lock changes (sections 76-1431.01 to 76-1431.04). Those rules stand apart from any sale.

The act sets its own court procedure for recovering possession. It runs from the action for possession in section 76-1440 through the complaint, summons, trial and writ of restitution, to appeal in section 76-1447. The Judicial Branch describes forcible entry and detainer as a proceeding to restore possession of land to a person who has been wrongfully deprived of it.

One detail catches owners who hold rentals in a company: except in Small Claims Court, a landlord that is a corporation or LLC cannot represent itself in court and must have an attorney.

If a case is open, talk to the attorney handling it before you sign a purchase agreement, and make sure the contract says whether the buyer takes the property occupied.

Selling a rental with a tenant inside is possible, and it goes more smoothly when the paperwork is in order. These steps help most owners.

  • Pull the signed lease, any addenda, and the rent ledger.
  • Confirm the deposit amount, any pet deposit, and where the money is held.
  • Make sure no notice of nonpayment or breach is half-finished, because the seven-day and thirty-day clocks run from written notice.
  • List open repair requests and complaints to a code office, since the retaliation rules apply.
  • Give the tenant written contact details for the new owner and manager at closing.

If the tenant is behind on rent or the home needs work, a buyer who purchases as-is can take the property in its current condition. Cash Home Buyers makes cash offers on Nebraska houses in that situation. This page is general information, not legal advice.

faqs.q: How much can a Nebraska landlord charge for a pet deposit?
faqs.a: Section 76-1416 allows a pet deposit of up to one-fourth of one month's periodic rent, on top of a security deposit that cannot exceed one month's rent. The cap does not apply to housing agencies under the Nebraska Housing Agency Act.

faqs.q: How long does a landlord have to give notice for unpaid rent?
faqs.a: Seven calendar days after written notice of nonpayment and of the intent to terminate. If the tenant does not pay in that time, the landlord may terminate under section 76-1431.

faqs.q: Who gets the deposit if the landlord sells?
faqs.a: The holder of the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends is bound by the deposit rules, so the new owner can be responsible. Seller and buyer should agree in writing at closing how the deposit is handled.

faqs.q: Can a tenant be evicted for complaining to the city about conditions?
faqs.a: Section 76-1439 prohibits retaliation, including bringing or threatening an action for possession, after a tenant complains to a code agency about a health or safety violation. Reasonable rent increases are still allowed.

faqs.q: Can an LLC landlord file an eviction case without a lawyer?
faqs.a: No. A landlord that is a corporation or LLC cannot represent itself in court, except in Small Claims Court, and must have an attorney.
